name: unshield
desc: Extract files from InstallShield cabinet files
why: Extracts files from InstallShield cabinets, a satisfying look into a forgotten Windows installer format.

brief.what_it_is: Unshield is a command-line tool and C library that lists and extracts files from InstallShield cabinet files (.cab archives that InstallShield installers use to store the files they install). You give it an InstallShield cabinet such as data1.cab and it either prints the archive's contents or writes the extracted files to a directory you name. The README says it extracts the Microsoft Cabinet Files nested inside the InstallShield cabinets, so the output is ordinary files you can then use on any OS. It is a from-scratch reimplementation rather than a wrapper around InstallShield's own code.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wanted to install Pocket PC applications from InstallShield installers on Linux or FreeBSD without needing Windows. The format is not officially documented, and the existing Windows tools (i5comp and i6comp) depended on InstallShield decompression code that was not open source.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the author used the existing i5comp and i6comp tools as a reference for the format, and found by running 'strings' over InstallShield's decompression code that it relied on zlib. Decompression therefore uses the open source zlib library, and the parsing logic is a clean reimplementation. The stated goals are MIT licensing, support for both little-endian and big-endian systems, a split between tool and library, support for InstallShield version 5 and later, and listing as well as extraction.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew installs it directly. To build from source the README asks for the standard CMake flow: cmake ., make, make install. No accounts, runtimes or configuration are mentioned. The 1.6.0 release notes mention a Windows build in GitHub Actions and MinGW and MSVC fixes, so Windows builds appear to be supported, but the README does not document them.
brief.standout: Unlike most extraction tools, this one exists because of a deliberately clean-room route: it reverse-engineers an undocumented 1990s Windows installer format by reading the older Windows tools and the strings in InstallShield's binaries. It is a small, focused C project with MIT licensing, and the README is candid about its history and limits.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The GitHub releases page lists 1.6.2 as Latest, dated 03 Apr (the year is not shown in the fetched text), with 1.6.1 on 02 Apr and 1.6.0 on 24 Mar. The 1.6.0 notes list a long run of CI, CMake and cleanup pull requests. The README itself has no staleness note.
brief.caveats: Old InstallShield cabinets may need the -O flag, and the README warns that -O selects a compression method, not a repair mode for damaged or unsupported cabinets. A failed run can still leave some files behind, so the exit status and error output must be checked. Support starts at InstallShield version 5, and the format is undocumented, so the tool may not handle every cabinet. The README also asks for a new output directory on each attempt. A PayPal donation link appears in the README. Licensed MIT, and the README's own summary is 'do as you like, but don't blame me if anything goes wrong'.

judge.reason: A small, obscure clean-room implementation for unpacking an undocumented legacy installer format makes old Windows software inspectable without Windows—a worthwhile reverse-engineering rabbit hole.

entry.title: unshield
entry.tldr: Unshield lists and extracts files from InstallShield cabinets, opening up a 1990s Windows installer format that was never officially documented.
entry.deeper_look:
Unshield is a command-line tool and C library for InstallShield cabinet files, the data1.cab-style archives that InstallShield installers use to carry the files they install. Point it at a cabinet and it either lists the contents or writes the files to a directory you choose. The README says it extracts the Microsoft Cabinet Files nested inside, so what comes out is ordinary files you can use on any OS.

The author wanted to install Pocket PC applications from InstallShield installers on Linux or FreeBSD without Windows. The format is not officially documented, and the existing Windows tools, i5comp and i6comp, depended on InstallShield decompression code that was not open source. The README puts it this way: "I could have modified i5comp and i6comp to run on other operating systems than Microsoft Windows, but I preferred to use them as a reference for this implementation."

The underlying idea is reverse engineering an undocumented format by reading what already exists. The author used the older tools as a reference, and ran `strings` over InstallShield's decompression code to discover that it relied on zlib. Decompression therefore uses open source zlib, and the parsing is a clean reimplementation. The stated goals are MIT licensing, little-endian and big-endian support, a split between tool and library, InstallShield version 5 and later, and both listing and extraction.

It is a good small door into how installers package files, and into how a format gets worked out from the outside.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage help; the README also points to a manual page for more options.
Lists the files inside an InstallShield cabinet without extracting anything.
Extracts the cabinet's contents into a directory named 'extracted'.

entry.whats_unique: It is a from-scratch, MIT-licensed reimplementation of an undocumented 1990s installer format, built by studying older Windows tools and the strings in InstallShield's binaries. The README is candid about that history and its limits.
entry.caveats: You need an InstallShield cabinet of your own to try it; very old ones may need the -O flag, which picks a compression method rather than repairing damaged files, and support starts at InstallShield version 5.
